passage:
In the school library, Gurleen reached across the table for the glue and knocked over her fountain-pen ink. A blue flood spread over Manjula's open science notebook, soaking two pages of careful diagrams.
Manjula gasped. Gurleen's face burned. Everyone at the table was looking. I'm so useless, she thought. I ruin everything.
She wanted to run out. Instead she grabbed tissues and pressed them on the pages, her hands shaking.
"I'm really sorry, Manjula. That was my fault. I'll copy the diagrams again for you tonight, neatly, with my best pens."
Manjula looked at the dripping page, then at Gurleen's red face. "Okay. The heart diagram's the hardest one."
"Then I'll do that one twice," Gurleen said, and Manjula almost smiled.
The next morning Gurleen handed over two fresh pages.

qa.q: What did the ink spill on?
qa.a: Manjula's open science notebook, soaking two pages of diagrams.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling right after the spill?
qa.a: Ashamed; her face burned and she thought she was useless and ruined everything.

qa.q: How did Gurleen turn shame into repair?
qa.a: She owned the mistake, apologised and offered to redraw the diagrams, then did it.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt watching Gurleen's reaction?
qa.a: Upset about the notebook, but softened by the sincere apology, so she almost smiled.

grounding: A girl whose face burns with shame after spilling ink on a friend's book apologises and offers to fix it.

passage:
Monday: Urmila was reading Mehak's favourite storybook at lunch when her ink pen leaked, leaving a blue blot across the cover and three pages. Her face burned. She shoved the book into her bag and avoided Mehak all afternoon. I'm a terrible friend, she kept thinking.
Tuesday: Urmila felt sick about it all day. At bedtime Mummy asked what was wrong, and Urmila told her. "You did a careless thing," Mummy said. "That doesn't make you a terrible person. What could fix it?"
Wednesday: Before class, Urmila held out the book with both hands. "Mehak, I spilled ink on it. I'm sorry I hid it. I'll help cover it, or ask Mummy about getting a new copy."
Mehak frowned at the blot, then shrugged. "It looks like a whale. Let's draw it a tail." They did.

qa.q: What did Mehak say the blot looked like?
qa.a: A whale.

qa.q: Why did Urmila avoid Mehak all afternoon on Monday?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, thinking she was a terrible friend, and hid the damaged book.

qa.q: What helped Urmila move from hiding to fixing?
qa.a: Mummy separating the careless act from who Urmila is; then Urmila apologised and offered to make it right.

qa.q: How did Mehak take the apology?
qa.a: She was a bit upset at first but forgiving, and turned the blot into a whale drawing.

grounding: A girl ashamed after spilling ink on her friend's book learns she did a bad thing without being bad, apologises and offers to fix it.

passage:
"Harish, did you see? Everyone laughed. The whole school."
"I saw you slip. I also saw you get up and finish the dance."
"I want to disappear. I'm never going on stage again."
"Jaya, remember when Mehra Sir's microphone squeaked in assembly? Everyone laughed for a minute. Does anybody talk about it now?"
"...No."
"Give it two days. They'll be laughing about something else."
"But they'll call me Jaya-Splat."
"Then they'll have to call me Harish-Splat too, because I'm sitting next to you at lunch."
Jaya gave a wet laugh. "You'd do that?"
"Already doing it. Come on, the samosas will finish."
She wiped her face, picked up her ghungroos and walked with him to the canteen.

qa.q: What did Harish see Jaya do after she slipped?
qa.a: Get up and finish the dance.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel after everyone laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated; she wanted to disappear and never go on stage again.

qa.q: How did Harish help Jaya cope?
qa.a: He reminded her how quickly people forget and stood by her by sitting with her at lunch.

qa.q: How does Harish see Jaya's fall?
qa.a: As a small slip followed by real courage, since she got up and finished.

grounding: A girl humiliated when the school laughs at her fall on stage is helped by a friend who stands by her and reminds her people soon forget.

passage:
I'm Naveen. Last term I had to read my essay aloud in class. I got stuck on the word "beautiful". B-b-b. My mouth just wouldn't open the rest of the way. Someone at the back snorted, and then the whole row laughed. My face was on fire. I wanted the floor to swallow me.
Somehow I finished and sat down, staring at my desk.
At break, Tejas sat next to me on the steps and handed me half his vada pav. He said, "Your essay was the best one. The part about the rain was really good." He didn't mention the laughing at all.
By the next week nobody even remembered. But I still remember Tejas on the steps.

qa.q: Which word did Naveen get stuck on?
qa.a: "beautiful".

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when the row laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated, with a burning face, wishing the floor would swallow Naveen up.

qa.q: What made Tejas's support so helpful?
qa.a: He sat with Naveen, shared his food and praised the essay without mentioning the laughing.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed remember the moment later?
qa.a: Most of them forgot it within a week; for them it was brief, though it hurt Naveen deeply.

grounding: A child laughed at for getting stuck on a word in class finds that most people forget soon and a friend standing by matters more.

passage: Tejas, you broke the remote and you're scared to tell your Amma? Let your Shalini Ammamma tell you something. When I was a girl, I took my mother's silver anklet to wear to a friend's wedding, without asking. On the way home I lost it in the paddy field. I searched till dark. My chest felt like a stone. For two days I said nothing, and every time Amma looked at me, I looked away. On the third night I couldn't bear it. I cried and told her everything. Amma was quiet. Then she wiped my face and said, "An anklet can be lost. My daughter cannot." The stone just melted. We searched together the next morning and never found it. But I never hid anything from her again. Go on, Tejas. Tell her.

qa.q: Where did young Shalini lose the anklet?
qa.a: In the paddy field.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel during the two silent days?
qa.a: Guilty and heavy; her chest felt like a stone and she could not look at Amma.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ammamma's story?
qa.a: Confessing to Amma on the third night, which ended the secret and brought forgiveness.

qa.q: How did Amma see the lost anklet compared with her daughter?
qa.a: The anklet could be lost, but her daughter mattered far more, so she forgave her.

grounding: A grandmother recalls confessing a mistake to her mother and feeling a weight lift when she was forgiven, learning that a mistake does not end love.

passage:
Diwali guests were arriving in thirty minutes, and the kitchen was chaos. Gautam was carrying Amma's special glass sweet dish, the one from her wedding, when it slipped. Crash. Laddoos and glass all over the floor.
His little brother Karthik froze. "Amma's going to be so angry," he whispered.
Gautam's heart hammered. He could push the pieces under the cupboard. Amma was so busy she might not notice for days.
Instead he went to the puja room door. "Amma, I broke your wedding dish. I'm sorry. It was me."
Amma closed her eyes for a second. Then she came and looked at the mess, and at his face. "Thank you for telling me straight away. Are your feet okay? Get the broom. We'll put the laddoos on the steel plate."
The weight in Gautam's chest lifted so fast he almost laughed.

qa.q: What did Gautam break?
qa.a: Amma's special glass sweet dish from her wedding.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel after Amma forgave him?
qa.a: Huge relief; the weight in his chest lifted so fast he almost laughed.

qa.q: Why was telling at once better than hiding the pieces, even with guests arriving?
qa.a: Amma could deal with it immediately, and the mistake was mended instead of becoming a secret.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when she closed her eyes for a second?
qa.a: Sad about losing her wedding dish, but she chose to value Gautam's honesty and safety more.

grounding: A boy confesses breaking his mother's special dish just before guests arrive, is forgiven quickly and feels a weight lift.

passage:
In Felix's classroom in Hamburg, the bean plants for the science project stood in a row on the windowsill. Racing to get his football at break, Felix swung his bag and knocked three pots onto the floor. Soil everywhere, stems snapped.
"Felix!" Ms. Noa's voice was sharp. "How many times have I said walk, don't run, near the experiments? Three weeks of work!"
Felix's face went hot. "It wasn't my fault, the pots were on the edge!" he shot back. Then he stared at his shoes. I'm useless, he thought. I break everything.
After break Ms. Noa spoke quietly. "I was sharp because I was upset. But you can fix some of it. Help me replant the ones that aren't broken."
Felix knelt and scooped soil. Two plants survived. Next time, he thought, I'll walk.

qa.q: How many pots did Felix knock onto the floor?
qa.a: Three pots.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling after Ms. Noa scolded him?
qa.a: Ashamed and defensive; he snapped back, then thought he was useless.

qa.q: What did Felix learn, and what did he do instead of giving up?
qa.a: To walk near the experiments; he helped replant the surviving beans.

qa.q: How did Ms. Noa see the moment she scolded Felix?
qa.a: She was upset about three weeks of work, which made her sharp, but later she offered him a way to help fix it.

grounding: A boy scolded sharply for a careless slip feels ashamed and defensive, then learns from it instead of deciding he is useless.

passage:
As class monitor, Uma had one job on Monday: collect the permission slips for the trip and give Rehana Ma'am the list. She missed two names.
"Uma!" Rehana Ma'am said sharply, in front of everyone. "Two children nearly got left off the bus list because of you. A monitor has to be careful."
Uma's cheeks flamed. "It's not my fault, they gave them late!" she said, too loudly. Someone giggled. She sat down with her arms crossed, thinking, I'm the worst monitor ever. I should just quit.
At lunch she looked at the list again. The two slips had actually come on time. She had just rushed.
After school she went to the staff room. "Ma'am, you were right. I rushed. Can I tick the names twice from now on?"
Rehana Ma'am's face softened. "That's exactly what a good monitor does."

qa.q: How many names did Uma miss?
qa.a: Two names.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she sat with her arms crossed?
qa.a: Ashamed and defensive, thinking she was the worst monitor and should quit.

qa.q: How did Uma learn from the scolding instead of deciding she was useless?
qa.a: She checked the list, admitted she had rushed, and offered to tick the names twice.

qa.q: How did Rehana Ma'am's view change when Uma came to the staff room?
qa.a: She softened and saw Uma acting like a good monitor.

grounding: A girl scolded sharply by her teacher feels ashamed and defensive, then listens to what she can learn and grows from it.

passage: Ira, you've been walking round the flowerpot corner all day. Is something hiding there? Before you answer, let your Vandana Mausi tell you a story. When I was nine, I knocked my father's reading glasses off the table and snapped the frame. I panicked and hid the pieces at the bottom of the rice tin. For four days my father searched everywhere, squinting at his newspaper, and I said nothing. Every night the secret sat on my chest like a sack of rice. On the fifth day Amma found the pieces while cooking. I burst into tears and told the whole thing. Papa said, "Glasses can be mended. I only wish you'd told me on day one." I felt so light, Ira. So, what's behind the flowerpot?

qa.q: Where did young Vandana hide the broken glasses?
qa.a: At the bottom of the rice tin.

qa.q: How did the secret feel to young Vandana?
qa.a: Heavy and guilty; it sat on her chest like a sack of rice every night.

qa.q: What choice in Mausi's story would have spared four days of worry?
qa.a: Telling Papa on day one, as he himself wished.

qa.q: How did Papa see the broken glasses?
qa.a: As something that could be mended; being told mattered more to him.

grounding: An aunt recalls hiding a broken object, how heavy the secret felt, and the relief of the truth coming out.

passage:
Mummy and Papa would be home from the market in twenty minutes. Ira was practising cartwheels in the drawing room, which was not allowed, when her foot clipped the blue vase from Nani. It shattered.
She swept the pieces into a newspaper and pushed it under her bed. Then she fluffed the curtains so the empty shelf looked less empty.
Her sister Himani came out of her room. "What was that crash?"
"Nothing."
But the nothing felt enormous. Ira's stomach twisted. When the doorbell rang, her legs felt like water. She opened the door, took a breath, and before anyone could put the bags down she said, "I broke Nani's vase doing cartwheels, and I hid it under my bed. I'm sorry."
Mummy sighed and hugged her. "Thank you for telling us yourself." Ira felt the knot in her stomach come undone.

qa.q: Where did Ira hide the pieces?
qa.a: Under her bed, wrapped in a newspaper.

qa.q: How did Ira feel while the pieces were hidden?
qa.a: Anxious and guilty; her stomach twisted and the "nothing" felt enormous.

qa.q: Why was telling at the door a good choice, even though she had hidden it first?
qa.a: It brought relief and showed Mummy and Papa that she could be trusted.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Ira said "Nothing"?
qa.a: Probably suspicious or curious, since she had clearly heard the crash.

grounding: A girl who breaks something at home and hides the pieces feels the weight of the secret and finds relief in telling the truth.

passage:
Monday: In art class, Rehana drew a kingfisher so real that Dilnaz half expected it to fly off the page. Dilnaz stared at her own lumpy bird. I could never do that, she thought.
Wednesday: At lunch Dilnaz finally asked, "How do you draw like that?"
Rehana laughed and pulled out a battered sketchbook. The first pages were full of wobbly, wonky birds. "I draw one every day. These were last year. They were terrible."
Dilnaz's mouth fell open. "These are worse than mine!"
"Exactly," Rehana grinned.
The next Monday: Dilnaz had a small notebook of her own now, with seven birds in it, one for each day. The seventh one had a proper beak. She showed Rehana, who drew a tiny star beside it.

qa.q: What did Rehana draw in art class?
qa.a: A kingfisher.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel looking at Rehana's kingfisher?
qa.a: Amazed, but also discouraged, thinking she could never draw like that.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do instead of giving up?
qa.a: She asked Rehana how she practises and started drawing a bird every day.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when Dilnaz asked?
qa.a: Pleased and happy to share her old wobbly birds to encourage Dilnaz.

grounding: A girl amazed by a classmate's drawing asks how she practises instead of deciding she could never do it.

passage: Charu, you say Anika sings like a bird and you can never sing like that? Sit, let your Hafsa Khala tell you something. When I was a girl in Lucknow, there was a girl in my class, Zeenat, whose voice made the whole assembly go still. The first time I heard her, I got goosebumps. And then I felt small, because when I sang, the dog next door howled. For weeks I just listened. One day I got brave and asked her, "How do you do it?" She laughed and said, "I sing on the roof every morning while I hang the washing. Come tomorrow." So I went. I was terrible. But I kept going, all winter. By spring we sang together at the school function. So go and ask Anika, Charu. Admiring someone is the first step.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat practise singing every morning?
qa.a: On the roof, while hanging the washing.

qa.q: How did young Hafsa feel the first time she heard Zeenat sing?
qa.a: Amazed, with goosebumps, and then small about her own singing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Khala's story?
qa.a: Asking Zeenat how she did it and going to practise with her every morning.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when Hafsa asked her?
qa.a: Flattered and happy; she laughed and invited Hafsa to come the next day.

grounding: An aunt recalls admiring a classmate's singing and asking how she practised instead of believing she never could.

passage:
At the village school's Independence Day fair, everyone crowded round Kashish's rangoli: a peacock in twelve colours. The headmaster clapped. The teachers took photos. "Kashish is so talented," people kept saying.
Hafsa stood at the edge, holding the small clay lamp she had made. Nobody looked at it. She felt invisible. A mean thought crept up: her mother probably helped her.
She almost said it aloud to her friend. Then she stopped. That wasn't fair, and it wasn't even why she felt bad. She felt bad because she wanted to be noticed too.
That evening Hafsa told Nani. "What do you love doing?" Nani asked. "Telling stories," Hafsa said. So Nani helped her write one down, and the next week Hafsa read it at assembly. The whole class laughed in all the right places.

qa.q: What did Kashish's rangoli show?
qa.a: A peacock in twelve colours.

qa.q: What was Hafsa really feeling at the fair?
qa.a: Envious and invisible; she wanted to be noticed too.

qa.q: How did Hafsa turn her envy into something useful?
qa.a: She stopped herself from running Kashish down and worked on her own strength, storytelling.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt if Hafsa had said her mother helped?
qa.a: Hurt and unfairly accused, when she had done nothing wrong.

grounding: A girl who feels invisible while a classmate's talent is praised notices her envy and works on her own strength instead of running the classmate down.

passage:
In Wanjiru's class in Lisbon, everyone talked about Ines. Ines had played piano at the school concert, and the video was going round every parent's phone. Even Wanjiru's own mother watched it twice.
Wanjiru felt invisible. At recess she heard herself say, "She only plays well because she has lessons every day," and the words tasted sour.
That night she lay awake. Why did she care so much? She didn't even like piano. What she loved was running. She was the fastest in class, but nobody filmed that.
The next week she asked the PE teacher about the district race and started training on the hill behind her building every morning. When Ines said, "Good luck at your race," Wanjiru blushed and said, "Your concert was really good."

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru train every morning?
qa.a: On the hill behind her building.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel about the praise for Ines?
qa.a: Envious and invisible, and her unkind words tasted sour afterwards.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru's envy show her, and how did she use it?
qa.a: It showed she wanted recognition for something she loves, so she began training for the district race.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt hearing Wanjiru's compliment?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, since she had wished Wanjiru good luck too.

grounding: A girl envious of a praised classmate sees what she herself cares about and works on her own strength instead of running the classmate down.

passage: Hrithik, your father keeps saying, "See your cousin, he came first"? I know that feeling. Let your Chinmay Mama tell you. My Appa used to hold up my cousin Sunil like a trophy. "Sunil got ninety-five. Sunil plays the veena. Why can't you be like Sunil?" Each time, something inside me went crunch. I stopped showing Appa my report card. One evening I gathered my courage and said, "Appa, I am trying. I'm not Sunil. I'm good at drawing, and nobody ever looks." Appa put his paper down and stared at me. The next day he asked to see my sketchbook. He didn't stop comparing overnight, but he started noticing. So, Hrithik, tell your father gently what you do well. Sometimes fathers need to be told.

qa.q: What instrument did cousin Sunil play?
qa.a: The veena.

qa.q: How did young Chinmay feel when Appa praised Sunil?
qa.a: Crushed; something inside him went crunch, and he stopped showing his report card.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mama's story?
qa.a: Telling Appa that he was trying in his own way and was good at drawing, which made Appa start noticing.

qa.q: How did Appa react when young Chinmay spoke up?
qa.a: He was taken aback, stared at his son, and the next day asked to see the sketchbook.

grounding: An uncle recalls feeling crushed when his father compared him to a cousin, and how saying he was trying in his own way made his father notice.

passage:
Results came out on a scorching afternoon, and the power had gone, so the whole family sat on the balcony fanning themselves. Mummy's phone buzzed: Nilesh, Harsha's cousin, had got 97 percent. "Look at Nilesh, so hard-working," Mummy said. "You got 81. Why can't you be more like him?"
Harsha felt crushed, like a paper cup underfoot. He wanted to shout, or hide in the dark bedroom. Instead he said quietly, "Mummy, I got 81 after failing maths last term. I'm doing my best, my way. Can you notice that?"
Mummy stopped fanning. She looked at him for a long moment. "Eighty-one... after failing. You're right." She pulled him close, sweaty and all. "I'm proud of that climb. I should have said it first."
Harsha's chest loosened in the heat.

qa.q: What percentage did Nilesh get?
qa.a: 97 percent.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Mummy compared him with Nilesh?
qa.a: Crushed, like a paper cup underfoot, wanting to shout or hide.

qa.q: How did Harsha respond wisely?
qa.a: He quietly pointed out his own climb from failing maths and asked Mummy to notice his effort.

qa.q: How did Mummy see things after Harsha spoke?
qa.a: She realised his climb from failing deserved praise and admitted she should have said it first.

grounding: A boy crushed when his mother compares him with a cousin says he is trying in his own way and asks her to notice his progress.

passage:
At the community centre's chess tournament, Dhruv won the under-twelve trophy. When his name was called the hall clapped, and Dhruv felt as if he were floating. He held the trophy up high and grinned at everyone.
On his way off the stage, he stopped. Gurleen Ma'am, his chess coach, was clapping at the back. She had given up her Saturdays for a whole year to teach him.
He ran down and put the trophy in her hands. "You taught me the knight fork," he said. "Half of this is yours."
Later, while the others ate samosas, a small boy sat alone at a board, stuck on a puzzle. Dhruv sat down opposite him. "Want to see a trick?" He showed him slowly. The boy's face lit up.

qa.q: Which trophy did Dhruv win?
qa.a: The under-twelve trophy.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when the hall clapped?
qa.a: Proud and joyful, as if he were floating.

qa.q: How did Dhruv keep his pride humble?
qa.a: He thanked Gurleen Ma'am by putting the trophy in her hands, then helped a younger boy with a puzzle.

qa.q: How might Gurleen Ma'am feel when Dhruv handed her the trophy?
qa.a: Touched and proud that he remembered her year of Saturdays.

grounding: A boy who wins a prize enjoys the applause and stays humble by thanking his coach and helping a younger learner.

passage:
Friday: Gargi won first prize in the inter-school singing competition. The applause rang in her ears all the way home, and she hummed her winning song at dinner three times.
Saturday: She heard her little brother Vikas in the next room, trying the same song, badly off-key. She almost laughed out loud. Then she remembered how she had squeaked two years ago, when Bhatt Sir first started teaching her. She went in and sat on the bed. "Try it lower. Like this."
Monday: Gargi took a card to school for Bhatt Sir. "Thank you for not giving up on my squeaky voice," she had written. That evening she and Vikas practised together. He was still a bit off-key, but grinning, and she clapped for him the loudest.

qa.q: What did Gargi write in the card for Bhatt Sir?
qa.a: "Thank you for not giving up on my squeaky voice."

qa.q: Why didn't Gargi laugh at Vikas?
qa.a: Remembering her own squeaky start made her feel understanding instead of superior.

qa.q: How did Gargi keep her pride healthy?
qa.a: She thanked her teacher and helped her brother learn the song.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt when Gargi clapped for him the loudest?
qa.a: Encouraged and happy, grinning even though he was still off-key.

grounding: A girl proud of winning a singing prize stays humble by thanking her teacher and helping her little brother learn.

passage:
Tuesday: Irawati's essay won the district prize. Her best friend Irfan, who had entered too, walked out of the hall without a word.
Wednesday: At lunch Irfan sat with other boys. When Irawati said hi, he just nodded. She felt confused, then guilty. Should she not have entered? Was winning a crime?
She almost stopped mentioning the prize at all. Instead she decided to give him space for a day, and stay kind.
Friday: She slipped a note into his bag: "Your essay about your grandfather made me cry. You matter more to me than any certificate. Carrom at five?"
At five, Irfan knocked. "Sorry," he mumbled, not looking up. "I was jealous. Congrats." She set up the board. He won the first game, and she didn't mind at all.

qa.q: What did Irawati's essay win?
qa.a: The district prize.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Irfan just nodded at lunch?
qa.a: Confused and guilty, wondering whether winning was a crime.

qa.q: How did Irawati handle Irfan's coldness?
qa.a: She gave him space, stayed kind, and sent a note praising his essay and inviting him to carrom.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling behind his coldness?
qa.a: He was jealous of her win, as he admitted when he apologised.

grounding: A girl whose friend goes cold after she wins a contest feels confused and guilty, gives him space and reminds him their friendship matters.

passage: Jeevan, your friend Aman won't talk to you since you won the quiz? Sit with your Jagdish Dadaji. When I was eleven, I won the Makar Sankranti kite contest in our mohalla. My best friend Mohan came second. That evening he didn't come to the terrace. The next day he walked past me as if I were a lamp-post. I felt terrible and confused, almost wished I had lost. My Bapuji said, "Don't take back your win, and don't chase him. Give him a few days, and be kind." So I waited. On the fourth day I took the prize, a huge red fighter kite, to his house. "It flies better with two," I said. He looked at it a long time. Then he fetched his manja. We flew it together till dark. So, Jeevan, stay kind and give Aman some time.

qa.q: What was the prize for the kite contest?
qa.a: A huge red fighter kite.

qa.q: How did young Jagdish feel when Mohan walked past him?
qa.a: Terrible and confused, almost wishing he had lost.

qa.q: What choice in Dadaji's story mended the friendship?
qa.a: Waiting a few days and then offering to fly the prize kite together.

qa.q: Why might Mohan have walked past as if Jagdish were a lamp-post?
qa.a: He was probably jealous and hurt about coming second.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a friend going cold after he won a contest, and how giving space and staying kind mended the friendship.
